title: A Unifying Response Time Analysis Framework for Dynamic Self-Suspending Tasks

extraction.paper_name: A Unifying Response Time Analysis Framework for Dynamic Self-Suspending Tasks
extraction.paper_description: This paper presents a unifying response time analysis framework for dynamic self-suspending tasks under preemptive fixed-priority scheduling on uniprocessor. It provides a rigorous proof for a new analysis that analytically dominates existing state-of-the-art methods (suspension as computation, release jitter, or blocking), demonstrating significant improvements in schedulability.

formal_description.statement: A sporadic self-suspending task tau_i is characterized by the tuple (C_i, S_i, D_i, T_i).

variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i
variables.S_i: worst-case self-suspension time of task i
variables.T_i: period (minimum inter-arrival time) of task i

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the fundamental parameters of a self-suspending task.

informal_sketch.intuition: Each task has a set of properties that define its behavior and requirements.
steps: C_i: How long the task actually computes.
S_i: How long the task might suspend itself, releasing the processor.
D_i: The maximum time allowed from release to completion.
T_i: The minimum time between consecutive releases of the same task.
key_insights: Self-suspension (S_i) is a distinct parameter from computation (C_i).
Tasks are sporadic, meaning T_i is a minimum inter-arrival time.

formal_description.statement: U_i = C_i / T_i

variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the utilization of a single task.

informal_sketch.intuition: Utilization represents the fraction of processor time a task demands over its period, assuming no suspension.
steps: Divide the task's computation time (C_i) by its period (T_i).
This gives a ratio representing the task's average processor demand.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_task_utilization(task_i):
    return task_i.C / task_i.T
key_insights: A higher utilization means a task demands more processor time.
This definition is standard for non-suspending tasks and is extended here.

formal_description.statement: The worst-case response time (WCRT) R_i of a task tau_i is the maximum response time among all its jobs.

variables.R_i: worst-case response time of task i

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum time a task can take to complete from its release.

informal_sketch.intuition: We need to find the longest possible time a task might take to finish after it's released, considering all possible interferences and suspensions.
steps: Simulate or analyze all possible scenarios for task tau_i's execution.
Identify the scenario where the time from release to completion is maximized.
This maximum duration is R_i.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_wcrt(task_i, task_set):
    # This is a complex calculation, often iterative
    # R_i = iterative_response_time_analysis(task_i, task_set)
    pass
key_insights: WCRT is a critical metric for schedulability.
It accounts for self-suspension, higher-priority interference, and blocking.

formal_description.statement: A schedulability test for a task tau_k is to verify whether its worst-case response time R_k is no more than its relative deadline D_k.

variables.R_k: worst-case response time of task k

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the condition for a task to be schedulable (i.e., meet its deadline).

informal_sketch.intuition: A task is schedulable if it always finishes before its deadline, even in the worst-case scenario.
steps: Calculate the worst-case response time (R_k) for the task.
Compare R_k with the task's relative deadline (D_k).
If R_k is less than or equal to D_k, the task is schedulable.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def is_task_schedulable(task_k, R_k):
    return R_k <= task_k.D
key_insights: This is the fundamental criterion for real-time system correctness.
The challenge lies in accurately calculating R_k.

formal_description.statement: hp_k = {tau_i | 1 <= i < k}

variables.hp_k: set of tasks with higher priority than task k
variables.k: index of the task under analysis

assumptions: Tasks are numbered in decreasing priority order (smaller index = higher priority).
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the set of tasks that can preempt task tau_k.

informal_sketch.intuition: When analyzing a task, we need to know which other tasks can interrupt its execution. These are the higher-priority tasks.
steps: Given a task tau_k, identify all tasks with an index smaller than k.
These tasks form the set hp_k.
key_insights: Interference from hp_k tasks is a major component of WCRT.
Lower priority tasks do not directly interfere with higher priority ones (Property 1).

formal_description.statement: For constrained-deadline tasks, D_i <= T_i.

variables.T_i: period (minimum inter-arrival time) of task i

formal_description.conclusion: A task model where the deadline is no later than the period.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is a common simplification in real-time analysis, meaning a job's deadline occurs before the next job of the same task is released.
steps: Check if for every task, its relative deadline is less than or equal to its period.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def is_constrained_deadline(task_i):
    return task_i.D <= task_i.T
key_insights: Simplifies analysis by avoiding carry-in jobs from previous periods for the same task.
The paper focuses on this model.

formal_description.statement: R_i <= D_i, for all tau_i | 1 <= i <= k-1.

variables.R_i: worst-case response time of task i
variables.k: index of the task under analysis

assumptions: Tasks are numbered in decreasing priority order.
formal_description.conclusion: All tasks with higher priority than tau_k are assumed to be schedulable.

informal_sketch.intuition: To analyze task tau_k, we first ensure that all tasks that can preempt it are themselves schedulable. This is a standard hierarchical approach in fixed-priority analysis.
steps: Before analyzing tau_k, perform schedulability tests for tau_1, tau_2, ..., tau_k-1.
If any of these higher-priority tasks are not schedulable (R_i > D_i), then the entire system might be unschedulable, or at least the analysis for tau_k is invalid under this assumption.
key_insights: This assumption allows us to use the properties of schedulable higher-priority tasks (e.g., R_i <= T_i) in the analysis of tau_k.
It's a prerequisite for many response time analyses.

results.identifier: Assumption: Stronger Higher Priority Tasks Schedulability

formal_description.statement: R_i <= D_i <= T_i, for all tau_i | 1 <= i <= k-1.

variables.R_i: worst-case response time of task i
variables.k: index of the task under analysis

assumptions: Tasks are numbered in decreasing priority order.
formal_description.conclusion: All tasks with higher priority than tau_k are assumed to be schedulable and have constrained deadlines.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is a stronger version of the previous assumption, explicitly stating that higher-priority tasks also adhere to the constrained-deadline model. This simplifies the analysis of their interference.
steps: Verify that R_i <= D_i for all higher-priority tasks.
Additionally, verify that D_i <= T_i for all higher-priority tasks.
key_insights: This assumption is used in the unifying analysis framework (Section V) to simplify workload calculations for higher-priority tasks.
It ensures that a job of a higher-priority task does not have its response time extend beyond its period, which is crucial for certain workload models.

results.identifier: Definition: Task Sets T_0 and T_1

formal_description.statement: A task tau_i is in T_0 if x_i is 0; otherwise, it is in T_1.

variables.x_i: binary variable (0 or 1) for task i

assumptions: x is an arbitrary vector assignment (x_1, ..., x_k-1) with x_i in {0, 1}.
formal_description.conclusion: Categorizes higher-priority tasks based on a binary decision variable x_i, which influences how their suspension is modeled.

informal_sketch.intuition: The new analysis framework uses a binary decision for each higher-priority task to determine how its self-suspension contributes to interference. T_0 tasks are treated one way, T_1 tasks another.
steps: For each higher-priority task tau_i, assign a binary value x_i.
If x_i is 0, tau_i belongs to set T_0.
If x_i is 1, tau_i belongs to set T_1.
key_insights: This binary choice (x_i) is central to the unifying framework, allowing it to adapt to different interference patterns.
The optimal choice of x_i needs to be found by iterating through all 2^(k-1) possibilities or using an optimization technique.

formal_description.statement: Q_x_i def = sum_j_from_i_to_k_minus_1 (S_j * x_j)

variables.Q_x_i: accumulated suspension term for task i based on vector x
variables.S_j: worst-case self-suspension time of task j
variables.x_j: binary variable (0 or 1) for task j
variables.k: index of the task under analysis

assumptions: x is an arbitrary vector assignment (x_1, ..., x_k-1) with x_j in {0, 1}.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a cumulative suspension term for tasks from i to k-1, weighted by the binary vector x.

informal_sketch.intuition: Q_x_i represents the total suspension time of tasks with priority higher than or equal to tau_i (up to tau_k-1) that are 'active' according to the x vector. It's a carry-in or jitter-like term.
steps: For a given task tau_i, iterate through all higher-priority tasks from tau_i up to tau_k-1.
If x_j for task tau_j is 1, add its suspension time S_j to the sum.
This sum is Q_x_i.
key_insights: This term captures the 'carry-in' effect of suspensions from higher-priority tasks.
The x_j variable allows selective inclusion of suspension times, which is key to the unifying framework.

dependencies: Definition: Task Sets T_0 and T_1

formal_description.statement: B_k = S_k + sum_i_from_1_to_k_minus_1 min(C_i, S_i)

variables.B_k: total blocking time for task k
variables.S_k: worst-case self-suspension time of task k
variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i
variables.S_i: worst-case self-suspension time of task i
variables.k: index of the task under analysis

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the total blocking time experienced by task tau_k, combining its own suspension and potential blocking from higher-priority tasks' suspensions.

informal_sketch.intuition: This model treats self-suspension as a form of blocking. Task tau_k blocks itself for S_k, and higher-priority tasks can 'block' tau_k for a limited duration due to their own suspensions.
steps: Start with tau_k's own suspension time S_k.
For each higher-priority task tau_i, calculate the minimum of its computation time C_i and its suspension time S_i.
Sum these minimums for all higher-priority tasks and add to S_k to get B_k.
key_insights: This is one of the state-of-the-art approaches for modeling self-suspension.
The min(C_i, S_i) term implies that a higher-priority task cannot block for longer than its computation or suspension, whichever is smaller.

formal_description.statement: A constrained-deadline task tau_k can be feasibly scheduled by a fixed-priority scheduling algorithm if there exists a time t such that 0 < t <= D_k, and C_k + S_k + sum_i_from_1_to_k_minus_1 (floor(t / T_i) * (C_i + S_i)) <= t.

variables.C_k: worst-case execution time of task k
variables.S_k: worst-case self-suspension time of task k
variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i
variables.S_i: worst-case self-suspension time of task i
variables.k: index of the task under analysis

formal_description.conclusion: Provides a schedulability test where suspension time is treated as additional computation time for all tasks.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the simplest approach: just add suspension time to computation time. Then, use standard response time analysis (like the busy-period equation) to check schedulability.
steps: For each task (including tau_k and higher-priority tasks), calculate an 'effective' computation time as C_i + S_i.

Iteratively search for a time 't' (up to D_k) where the total workload (tau_k's effective computation plus interference from higher-priority tasks' effective computation) is less than or equal to 't'.
If such a 't' exists, tau_k is schedulable.
key_insights: This method is often pessimistic because suspension time does not always directly contribute to interference in the same way as computation.
It's a baseline for comparison.

formal_description.statement: A task tau_k with a constrained deadline can be feasibly scheduled under fixed-priority if there exists a time t such that 0 < t <= D_k, and C_k + S_k + sum_i_from_1_to_k_minus_1 (floor((t + R_i - C_i) / T_i) * C_i) <= t.

variables.C_k: worst-case execution time of task k
variables.S_k: worst-case self-suspension time of task k
variables.R_i: worst-case response time of task i
variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i
variables.k: index of the task under analysis

assumptions: R_i - C_i is a safe upper bound for release jitter of task i.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a schedulability test where the impact of higher-priority tasks' self-suspension is modeled as release jitter.

informal_sketch.intuition: Self-suspension of a higher-priority task can delay its completion, effectively making its subsequent jobs appear 'jittered'. This jitter increases interference.
steps: For task tau_k, its own suspension S_k is treated as computation.
For each higher-priority task tau_i, calculate its effective release jitter as R_i - C_i.
Use this jitter in the standard response time equation to calculate interference from tau_i.
Search for a time 't' (up to D_k) where the total workload (tau_k's effective computation plus jitter-affected interference) is less than or equal to 't'.
If such a 't' exists, tau_k is schedulable.
key_insights: This approach can be more accurate than suspension-oblivious for higher-priority tasks.
The jitter term R_i - C_i accounts for the maximum delay a job can experience before its actual execution starts, due to its own suspension and higher-priority interference.

formal_description.statement: A constrained-deadline task tau_k can be feasibly scheduled under fixed-priority scheduling if there exists a time t such that 0 < t <= D_k, and C_k + B_k + sum_i_from_1_to_k_minus_1 (floor(t / T_i) * C_i) <= t.

variables.C_k: worst-case execution time of task k
variables.B_k: total blocking time for task k
variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i
variables.k: index of the task under analysis

formal_description.conclusion: Provides a schedulability test where self-suspension is modeled as a blocking term, and higher-priority tasks' interference is calculated without considering their suspensions directly.

informal_sketch.intuition: This approach aggregates all suspension-related delays into a single blocking term (B_k) for the task under analysis. Higher-priority tasks then interfere as if they were non-suspending.
steps: Calculate the total blocking time B_k for task tau_k (which includes its own suspension and limited blocking from higher-priority tasks' suspensions).
Use B_k in the standard response time equation, where higher-priority tasks interfere only with their computation times (C_i).
Search for a time 't' (up to D_k) where the total workload (tau_k's computation plus B_k plus interference from higher-priority tasks) is less than or equal to 't'.
If such a 't' exists, tau_k is schedulable.
key_insights: This method separates the suspension impact into a blocking term, simplifying the interference calculation.
The paper provides a formal proof for the correctness of this test, which was previously unproven.

formal_description.statement: In a preemptive fixed-priority schedule, the lower-priority jobs do not impact the schedule of the higher-priority jobs.
formal_description.conclusion: Lower priority tasks cannot delay or change the execution of higher priority tasks.

informal_sketch.intuition: By definition of preemptive fixed-priority scheduling, a higher-priority task always gets the processor if it's ready, regardless of what lower-priority tasks are doing.
steps: If a higher-priority task becomes ready, it immediately preempts any lower-priority task currently running.
Therefore, the execution of lower-priority tasks has no direct effect on when higher-priority tasks run or finish.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def is_higher_priority_unaffected(hp_task, lp_task):
    # In a fixed-priority system, if hp_task.priority > lp_task.priority
    # then hp_task's schedule is independent of lp_task's presence.
    return True
key_insights: This is a fundamental principle of fixed-priority scheduling.
It allows us to analyze tasks in isolation from lower-priority interference.

formal_description.statement: In a preemptive fixed-priority schedule, if the worst-case response time of task tau_i is no more than its period T_i, removing a job of task tau_i does not affect the schedule of any other jobs of task tau_i.

variables.R_i: worst-case response time of task i

assumptions: R_i <= T_i (task tau_i is schedulable within its period)
formal_description.conclusion: Jobs of a schedulable task tau_i do not interfere with other jobs of the same task.

informal_sketch.intuition: If a task always finishes within its period, then by the time its next job arrives, the previous one is already done. So, jobs of the same task don't overlap or interfere.
steps: Assume a job J_i,j of task tau_i is released at r_i,j and finishes at f_i,j.
Since R_i <= T_i, we know f_i,j <= r_i,j + T_i.
The next job J_i,j+1 is released at r_i,j+1 >= r_i,j + T_i.
This means f_i,j <= r_i,j+1, so J_i,j completes before J_i,j+1 is released.
Therefore, removing J_i,j (or any other job) won't affect the timing of other jobs of tau_i.
key_insights: This lemma is crucial for simplifying the analysis by allowing us to focus on a single job of the task under analysis (J_k) without worrying about its previous or subsequent jobs.
It relies on the constrained-deadline assumption (R_i <= T_i).

formal_description.statement: The response time of J_k in Psi_k is the same as the response time of J_k in Psi.

variables.J_k: the job of task k under analysis
variables.Psi_k: a modified schedule where lower-priority tasks are removed, only one job of tau_k is considered, and tau_k's suspension is converted to computation (C_k_prime = C_k + S_k).

assumptions: R_k <= T_k (for the job J_k under analysis)
formal_description.conclusion: Simplifying the schedule by removing lower-priority tasks and other jobs of tau_k, and converting tau_k's suspension to computation, does not change J_k's response time.

informal_sketch.intuition: We can simplify the system to focus only on the task under analysis and its higher-priority interferers. Lower-priority tasks don't matter, and if tau_k is schedulable within its period, its other jobs don't matter either.
steps: Start with the original schedule Psi.
Remove all jobs of tasks tau_k+1, ..., tau_n (lower priority). By Property 1, this doesn't affect J_k.
Remove all jobs of tau_k except J_k. By Lemma 1 (assuming R_k <= T_k), this doesn't affect J_k.
Convert J_k's suspension time S_k into computation time, so its effective computation is C_k_prime = C_k + S_k. This is a common modeling technique for the task under analysis.
The resulting schedule Psi_k has the same response time for J_k as Psi.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def create_psi_k(original_schedule, J_k, task_k):
    psi_k_schedule = deepcopy(original_schedule)
    # 1. Remove lower priority tasks
    for lp_task in get_lower_priority_tasks(task_k):
        psi_k_schedule.remove_task(lp_task)
    # 2. Remove other jobs of task_k (if R_k <= T_k)
    psi_k_schedule.keep_only_job(J_k)
    # 3. Convert J_k's suspension to computation
    J_k.C_effective = task_k.C + task_k.S
    J_k.S = 0
    return psi_k_schedule
key_insights: This is the basic step in constructing a 'critical instant' for self-suspending tasks.
It allows us to analyze a simplified system while preserving the WCRT of J_k.

formal_description.statement: The response time of J_k in Psi_j is the same as the response time of J_k in Psi_j+1.

variables.J_k: the job of task k under analysis

assumptions: R_j <= D_j <= T_j for j = 1, ..., k-1
formal_description.conclusion: Iteratively reducing the schedule by removing or modifying jobs of higher-priority tasks (tau_j) does not change J_k's response time.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma describes an inductive step: how to simplify the schedule for one higher-priority task (tau_j) without affecting J_k's response time. It handles different scenarios based on whether tau_j is in T_0 or T_1 and its completion status.
steps: Start with schedule Psi_j+1.
Identify the last job J_j of task tau_j released before a certain time t_j+1.
**Case 0 (No jobs before t_j+1):** Psi_j is identical to Psi_j+1.
**Case 1 (tau_j in T_1, J_j not completed by t_j+1):** Remove jobs of tau_j before J_j. J_j is kept. t_j is set to J_j's release time.
**Case 2 (tau_j in T_1, J_j completed by t_j+1):** Remove jobs of tau_j before t_j+1. J_j is removed. t_j is set to t_j+1.
**Case 3 (tau_j in T_0):** Remove jobs of tau_j before t_j+1. J_j is removed. An artificial job with J_j's residual workload is released at t_j+1. t_j is set to t_j+1.
In all cases, the interference on J_k remains equivalent, so J_k's response time is unchanged.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def create_psi_j_from_psi_j_plus_1(psi_j_plus_1, task_j, t_j_plus_1, x_j):
    psi_j = deepcopy(psi_j_plus_1)
    # ... logic for Case 0, 1, 2, 3 based on task_j's status and x_j ...
    # The key is that the *interference* on J_k remains the same.
    return psi_j
key_insights: This iterative reduction process is the core of the proof for the unifying framework.
The distinction between T_0 and T_1 tasks (via x_j) determines how their residual workload and release patterns are handled to maximize interference on J_k.

dependencies: Definition: Task Sets T_0 and T_1
Assumption: Stronger Higher Priority Tasks Schedulability

formal_description.statement: The response time of job J_k in Psi_1 is the same as the response time of J_k in Psi.

variables.J_k: the job of task k under analysis
variables.Psi_1: the final reduced schedule after iteratively applying the reduction steps for all higher-priority tasks.

assumptions: R_i <= D_i <= T_i for all tau_i | 1 <= i <= k
formal_description.conclusion: The iterative reduction process (from Psi to Psi_k, then Psi_k to Psi_k-1, ..., to Psi_1) preserves the worst-case response time of J_k.

informal_sketch.intuition: Since each step of the reduction (Lemma 2 and Lemma 3) preserves J_k's response time, the cumulative effect of all reductions also preserves it.
steps: Start with the original schedule Psi.
Apply Lemma 2 to get Psi_k, preserving J_k's response time.
Inductively apply Lemma 3 for j = k-1 down to 1, transforming Psi_j+1 into Psi_j, each time preserving J_k's response time.
The final schedule Psi_1 therefore has the same response time for J_k as the original Psi.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def get_final_reduced_schedule(original_schedule, J_k, task_set):
    psi_k = create_psi_k(original_schedule, J_k, task_set[k-1])
    psi_current = psi_k
    for j in range(k - 2, -1, -1): # Iterate from k-1 down to 1
        psi_current = create_psi_j_from_psi_j_plus_1(psi_current, task_set[j], t_j_plus_1_from_previous_step, x_vector[j])
    return psi_current # This is Psi_1
key_insights: This lemma validates the entire schedule reduction process, ensuring that the analysis performed on Psi_1 is equivalent to analyzing the original system.
It sets the stage for deriving the response time bounds from Psi_1.

formal_description.statement: For j = 1, 2, ..., k-1, sigma_j = x_j * sigma_j <= x_j * S_j.

variables.sigma_j: amount of idle time in [t_j, t_j+1) in schedule Psi_1
variables.x_j: binary variable (0 or 1) for task j
variables.S_j: worst-case self-suspension time of task j
variables.t_j: start time of interval for task j in Psi_1
variables.t_j+1: end time of interval for task j in Psi_1

assumptions: x_j determines if tau_j is in T_0 or T_1
formal_description.conclusion: The idle time introduced by task tau_j's suspension in a specific interval is bounded by its suspension time S_j, but only if x_j is 1 (i.e., tau_j is in T_1).

informal_sketch.intuition: When we construct Psi_1, if a task tau_j (with x_j=1) is active and not completed in an interval, it can suspend, causing idle time. This idle time is at most its total suspension S_j. If x_j=0, or if tau_j completes, no idle time is attributed to it in this specific way.
steps: Consider the interval [t_j, t_j+1) in Psi_1.

If x_j = 1 (tau_j in T_1) and tau_j's job is not completed by t_j+1 (Case 1 of Lemma 3), then t_j is set to the job's release time. Any idle time in [t_j, t_j+1) is due to tau_j's suspension, bounded by S_j.
If x_j = 0 (tau_j in T_0) or tau_j completes (Case 2), or no jobs before t_j+1 (Case 0), then t_j is set to t_j+1, meaning the interval [t_j, t_j+1) has zero length, so sigma_j = 0.
Combining these, sigma_j is either 0 or bounded by S_j, effectively sigma_j <= x_j * S_j.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def bound_sigma_j(j, t_j, t_j_plus_1, x_j, S_j):
    if x_j == 1 and (t_j_plus_1 - t_j) > 0: # Corresponds to Case 1
        # sigma_j is the actual idle time due to tau_j's suspension in [t_j, t_j+1)
        # This is bounded by S_j
        return min(actual_idle_time_in_interval(t_j, t_j_plus_1), S_j)
    else: # Corresponds to Case 0, 2, 3
        return 0
key_insights: This lemma quantifies the idle time introduced by self-suspension in the reduced schedule.
The x_j variable acts as a switch: only tasks in T_1 contribute to this specific type of idle time (sigma_j).

dependencies: Definition: Task Sets T_0 and T_1

formal_description.statement: For i = 1, 2, ..., k-1, for all t | t_i < t <= t_i+1, idle(t_1, t) <= sum_j_from_1_to_i (x_j * sigma_j) <= sum_j_from_1_to_i (x_j * S_j).

variables.idle_t_1_t: total idle time in interval [t_1, t)
variables.t_i: start time of interval for task i in Psi_1
variables.t_i+1: end time of interval for task i in Psi_1
variables.x_j: binary variable (0 or 1) for task j
variables.sigma_j: amount of idle time in [t_j, t_j+1) in Psi_1
variables.S_j: worst-case self-suspension time of task j

formal_description.conclusion: The total idle time in an interval [t_1, t) is bounded by the sum of sigma_j (or S_j) for tasks up to the current interval.

informal_sketch.intuition: The total idle time up to a point 't' is the sum of idle times in all preceding sub-intervals. Each sub-interval's idle time is bounded by sigma_j (or S_j) if the corresponding task is in T_1.
steps: The total idle time idle(t_1, t) is the sum of idle times in intervals [t_1, t_2), [t_2, t_3), ..., [t_i, t).
Each of these idle times is sigma_j for j < i, and the idle time in [t_i, t) is also bounded by sigma_i (or S_i).
Applying Lemma 5, each sigma_j is bounded by x_j * S_j.
Thus, the total idle time is bounded by the sum of x_j * S_j for relevant tasks.
key_insights: This corollary provides an upper bound on the total idle time that can occur due to self-suspension in the reduced schedule.
It directly uses the x_j variables to determine which tasks' suspensions contribute to this idle time.

formal_description.statement: For all t | t_k <= t < f_k, the (accumulative) amount of time that task tau_k is executed from t_k to t is exec_k(t_k, t) < C_k.

variables.t_k: release time of J_k in Psi_1
variables.f_k: finishing time of J_k in Psi_1
variables.exec_k_t_k_t: accumulative execution time of task k in [t_k, t)
variables.C_k: worst-case execution time of task k

assumptions: J_k is the job of task k under analysis
formal_description.conclusion: Before J_k finishes, its accumulated execution time must be less than its total computation time.

informal_sketch.intuition: A task cannot have completed its full computation before its finishing time. So, at any point before it finishes, it must have executed less than its total required computation.
steps: Consider the interval from J_k's release (t_k) up to any time 't' before its completion (f_k).
The amount of time J_k has executed in this interval, exec_k(t_k, t), must be strictly less than C_k.
If it were equal to C_k, J_k would have finished at or before 't', contradicting 't < f_k'.
key_insights: This is a basic property of execution time and completion.
It's used in the busy-period analysis to ensure that the task under analysis is still active.

formal_description.statement: W_1_j(delta) def = floor(delta / T_j) * C_j + min(delta - floor(delta / T_j) * T_j, C_j).

variables.W_1_j_delta: workload function for task j over interval delta
variables.C_j: worst-case execution time of task j

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum execution time that a sporadic task (without self-suspension) can demand in an interval of length delta, assuming a critical instant.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the standard workload function for a non-suspending sporadic task. It calculates the computation from full jobs released within delta, plus any partial job that might be released at the start of the interval.
steps: Calculate the number of full jobs of tau_j that can be released in an interval of length delta: floor(delta / T_j).
Multiply this by C_j to get the computation from full jobs.
Add the computation from a potential 'carry-in' job: this is the minimum of C_j and the remaining time in delta after accounting for full periods (delta mod T_j).
Sum these two parts.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def W_1_j(delta, T_j, C_j):
    num_jobs = math.floor(delta / T_j)
    work_from_full_jobs = num_jobs * C_j
    remaining_time = delta % T_j
    work_from_partial_job = min(remaining_time, C_j)
    return work_from_full_jobs + work_from_partial_job
key_insights: This function is a cornerstone of response time analysis for sporadic tasks.
It represents the maximum interference a non-suspending task can generate.

formal_description.statement: If task tau_j is in T_1, then for all delta >= 0 we have exec_j(t_j, t_j + delta) <= W_1_j(delta).

variables.exec_j_t_j_t_j_plus_delta: accumulative execution time of task j in [t_j, t_j + delta)
variables.W_1_j_delta: workload function for task j over interval delta

formal_description.conclusion: For tasks in T_1, their execution time in Psi_1 is bounded by the standard non-suspending workload function.

informal_sketch.intuition: When x_j = 1, the construction of Psi_1 (Case 1 or 2 of Lemma 3) ensures that there is no 'residual workload' from tau_j at t_j. Thus, tau_j behaves like a standard sporadic task from t_j onwards, and its workload is bounded by W_1_j(delta).
steps: Recall that if tau_j is in T_1, then in Psi_1, either all jobs before t_j are removed (Case 2) or the job J_j is kept but its release is t_j (Case 1).
In both cases, there is no 'carry-in' workload from a job released *before* t_j that is still active *at* t_j.
Therefore, the maximum execution time tau_j can demand in an interval starting at t_j is given by the standard sporadic workload function W_1_j(delta).
key_insights: This lemma simplifies the workload calculation for T_1 tasks, treating them as non-suspending for interference purposes.
The suspension of T_1 tasks is instead captured by the sigma_j term (idle time).

dependencies: Definition: Task Sets T_0 and T_1

formal_description.statement:
W_0_j(delta, c_star_j) = 
    { W_1_j(delta) if c_star_j = 0 
    ; delta if c_star_j > 0 and delta <= c_star_j 
    ; c_star_j if c_star_j > 0 and c_star_j < delta <= rho_j 
    ; c_star_j + W_1_j(delta - rho_j) if c_star_j > 0 and rho_j < delta }
where rho_j = (T_j - R_j + c_star_j).

variables.W_0_j_delta_c_star_j: workload function for task j over interval delta with residual workload c_star_j
variables.c_star_j: residual workload of task j at the start of the interval
variables.rho_j: time until the next job of task j can be released after accounting for residual workload
variables.R_j: worst-case response time of task j
variables.W_1_j_delta: workload function for task j over interval delta (non-suspending)

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum execution time that a task in T_0 can demand in an interval of length delta, considering a potential residual workload at the start of the interval.

informal_sketch.intuition: For tasks in T_0, their suspension is modeled as a 'blocking' or 'carry-in' effect. If there's a residual workload (c_star_j) from a previous job, it executes first. Then, new jobs arrive, but not before a certain 'rho_j' time, which accounts for the task's response time and period.
steps: **No residual workload (c_star_j = 0):** Behaves like a standard sporadic task, so use W_1_j(delta).
**Residual workload (c_star_j > 0):**
- If delta is very short (<= c_star_j), only the residual workload executes, up to delta.
- If delta is longer but still within rho_j (c_star_j < delta <= rho_j), only the residual workload c_star_j executes. No new jobs arrive yet.
- If delta is very long (> rho_j), the residual workload c_star_j executes, and then new jobs arrive, contributing W_1_j(delta - rho_j) from the remaining time.
key_insights: This function captures the 'carry-in' effect of a partially executed job for tasks in T_0.
The rho_j term ensures that the minimum inter-arrival time and the task's response time are respected when considering subsequent job releases.

formal_description.statement: W_0_j(delta) def = W_0_j(delta, C_j).

variables.W_0_j_delta: workload function for task j over interval delta (worst-case residual workload)
variables.C_j: worst-case execution time of task j

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the worst-case workload for a task in T_0 by assuming its residual workload is its full computation time C_j.

informal_sketch.intuition: To get an upper bound on the workload for a T_0 task, we assume the worst possible residual workload at the start of the interval, which is its full computation time C_j.
steps: Substitute c_star_j with C_j in the W_0_j(delta, c_star_j) definition.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def W_0_j_worst_case(delta, T_j, R_j, C_j):
    return W_0_j(delta, C_j, T_j, R_j, C_j)
key_insights: This simplified version is used to derive a safe upper bound for the interference from T_0 tasks.
It represents the maximum possible interference from a T_0 task, including a 'carry-in' job.

formal_description.statement: If tau_j is in T_0, then for all delta >= 0 we have exec_j(t_j, t_j + delta) <= W_0_j(delta, c_star_j).

variables.exec_j_t_j_t_j_plus_delta: accumulative execution time of task j in [t_j, t_j + delta)
variables.W_0_j_delta_c_star_j: workload function for task j over interval delta with residual workload c_star_j
variables.c_star_j: residual workload of task j at the start of the interval

formal_description.conclusion: For tasks in T_0, their execution time in Psi_1 is bounded by the workload function W_0_j(delta, c_star_j), which accounts for residual workload.

informal_sketch.intuition: When x_j = 0, the construction of Psi_1 (Case 3 of Lemma 3) involves replacing a partially completed job with an artificial job at t_j+1 (which becomes t_j). This artificial job carries the residual workload c_star_j. The lemma states that the maximum execution from such a task is bounded by W_0_j(delta, c_star_j).
steps: Recall that if tau_j is in T_0, then in Psi_1, any job of tau_j released before t_j is removed, and an artificial job with residual workload c_star_j is released at t_j.
This artificial job behaves like the original job from t_j onwards.
The earliest a *new* job of tau_j can arrive after this artificial job is at t_j + rho_j, where rho_j accounts for the period and response time.
The W_0_j(delta, c_star_j) function correctly models the execution from this artificial job and subsequent jobs.
key_insights: This lemma provides the workload model for T_0 tasks, which explicitly considers a 'carry-in' workload from a previous job.
This is distinct from the T_1 model where suspension contributes to idle time.

dependencies: Definition: Task Sets T_0 and T_1
Assumption: Stronger Higher Priority Tasks Schedulability

formal_description.statement: For all delta >= 0, W_0_j(delta) >= W_0_j(delta, c_star_j).

variables.W_0_j_delta: worst-case workload function for task j over interval delta (with c_star_j = C_j)
variables.W_0_j_delta_c_star_j: workload function for task j over interval delta with residual workload c_star_j
variables.c_star_j: residual workload of task j at the start of the interval

formal_description.conclusion: The workload function W_0_j(delta) (assuming full residual workload C_j) provides an upper bound for W_0_j(delta, c_star_j) (with any residual workload c_star_j).

informal_sketch.intuition: Having more residual workload at the start of an interval can only increase or keep the same the total work done in that interval. So, assuming the maximum possible residual workload (C_j) gives the worst-case.
steps: Compare the cases in the definition of W_0_j(delta, c_star_j) when c_star_j is replaced by C_j.
If c_star_j = 0, W_0_j(delta, 0) = W_1_j(delta). W_0_j(delta, C_j) will be >= W_1_j(delta) (as C_j > 0).
If c_star_j > 0, increasing c_star_j to C_j (where C_j >= c_star_j) will either increase the initial execution or shift the start of subsequent jobs later, but the total workload will not decrease.
Therefore, W_0_j(delta, C_j) is always greater than or equal to W_0_j(delta, c_star_j).
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def is_W0_worst_case_upper_bound(delta, c_star_j, C_j, T_j, R_j):
    return W_0_j_worst_case(delta, T_j, R_j, C_j) >= W_0_j(delta, c_star_j, T_j, R_j, C_j)
key_insights: This lemma allows us to use the simpler W_0_j(delta) (with C_j as residual workload) as a safe upper bound for interference from T_0 tasks, regardless of their actual residual workload.
It simplifies the overall response time analysis.

formal_description.statement:
For all t | t_i <= t < t_i+1 where i = 1, 2, ..., k-1, sum_j_from_1_to_i (x_j * (W_1_j(t - t_j) + sigma_j) + (1 - x_j) * W_0_j(t - t_j)) >= t - t_1. (10)
And, for all t | t_k <= t < f_k, C_k + sum_j_from_1_to_k_minus_1 (x_j * (W_1_j(t - t_j) + sigma_j) + (1 - x_j) * W_0_j(t - t_j)) > t - t_1. (11)

variables.t_i: start time of interval for task i in Psi_1
variables.t_k: release time of J_k in Psi_1
variables.f_k: finishing time of J_k in Psi_1
variables.C_k: worst-case execution time of task k
variables.x_j: binary variable (0 or 1) for task j
variables.W_1_j_t_minus_t_j: workload function for task j over interval (t - t_j)
variables.sigma_j: amount of idle time in [t_j, t_j+1) in Psi_1
variables.W_0_j_t_minus_t_j: worst-case workload function for task j over interval (t - t_j)

assumptions: J_k is the job of task k under analysis
formal_description.conclusion: These inequalities relate the total workload (computation + idle time) in an interval [t_1, t) to the length of the interval itself, providing a fundamental condition for the schedule.

informal_sketch.intuition: The total time in any interval [t_1, t) is either spent executing tasks or is idle. This lemma states that the sum of all higher-priority task workloads (modeled differently based on x_j) plus the idle time must be at least the length of the interval, and for the task under analysis, its own execution plus higher-priority interference must be greater than the interval length if it hasn't finished.
steps: Start with the basic equation: idle(t_1, t) + exec(t_1, t) = t - t_1.
Substitute idle(t_1, t) with its upper bound from Corollary 2: sum_j_from_1_to_i (x_j * sigma_j).
Substitute exec(t_1, t) with the sum of individual task executions exec_j(t_j, t).
For each task tau_j, use Lemma 7 (if x_j=1) or Lemma 8 (if x_j=0, using Lemma 9 to use W_0_j(delta)) to bound exec_j(t_j, t).
Combine these to get Eq. (10).
For Eq. (11), add C_k (from Lemma 6) to the execution term and note that idle(t_k, t) = 0 for tau_k's execution, leading to a strict inequality because tau_k is still executing.
key_insights: These inequalities are the core mathematical expressions that must hold for any valid schedule.
They combine the different workload models (W_1_j, W_0_j) and idle time (sigma_j) based on the x_j vector.
The strict inequality in (11) indicates that if J_k has not finished, the demand must exceed the available time.

dependencies: Definition: Task Sets T_0 and T_1

formal_description.statement: For any delta > 0, we have W_1_j(delta) <= floor(delta / T_j) * C_j (15) and W_0_j(delta) <= floor((delta + R_j - C_j) / T_j) * C_j (16).

variables.W_1_j_delta: workload function for task j over interval delta (non-suspending)
variables.W_0_j_delta: worst-case workload function for task j over interval delta
variables.C_j: worst-case execution time of task j
variables.R_j: worst-case response time of task j

formal_description.conclusion: Provides simpler, looser upper bounds for the workload functions W_1_j(delta) and W_0_j(delta).

informal_sketch.intuition: These are common approximations or upper bounds for workload functions. For W_1_j, it's simply the number of full jobs times their computation. For W_0_j, the (R_j - C_j) term acts like a jitter, increasing the number of jobs that can arrive.
steps: For W_1_j(delta): The exact formula includes a min(remaining_time, C_j) term. Replacing this with C_j and then using (delta/T_j) * C_j as an upper bound is a standard simplification.

For W_0_j(delta): The proof shows that W_0_j(delta) <= C_j + W_1_j(delta - (T_j - R_j + C_j)). By substituting the upper bound for W_1_j and simplifying, the expression (delta + R_j - C_j) / T_j * C_j is derived. The floor is added for consistency with job counts.
key_insights: These bounds are used to simplify the complex inequalities from Lemma 10 into a form that resembles the final response time equation.
The (R_j - C_j) term in W_0_j's bound explicitly models the maximum jitter for tasks in T_0.

formal_description.statement: t_star_i def = t_1 if i = 1; t_star_i_minus_1 + x_i_minus_1 * sigma_i_minus_1 if i = 2, 3, ..., k.

variables.t_star_i: artificial time point for task i
variables.x_i_minus_1: binary variable (0 or 1) for task i-1
variables.sigma_i_minus_1: amount of idle time in [t_i-1, t_i) in Psi_1

formal_description.conclusion: Defines a sequence of artificial time points that are less than or equal to the actual time points t_i in Psi_1, by accumulating only the 'active' idle times.

informal_sketch.intuition: The actual time points t_i are complex. We define simpler 'artificial' time points t_star_i by accumulating only the idle times (sigma_j) that are 'activated' by x_j=1. This helps in simplifying the workload equations.
steps: t_star_1 is simply t_1.
For subsequent t_star_i, add the previous t_star_i-1 with the idle time sigma_i-1, but only if x_i-1 is 1. If x_i-1 is 0, then sigma_i-1 is effectively ignored for this accumulation.
key_insights: This definition is a clever trick to simplify the workload equations by 'absorbing' the sigma_j terms into the time axis.
It allows the response time equation to be expressed in terms of a single variable (theta = t - t_star_k).

dependencies: Definition: Task Sets T_0 and T_1

formal_description.statement: t_star_i <= t_i for i = 1, 2, ..., k.

variables.t_star_i: artificial time point for task i
variables.t_i: actual time point for task i in Psi_1

formal_description.conclusion: The artificial time points t_star_i are always less than or equal to their corresponding actual time points t_i.

informal_sketch.intuition: The actual time points t_i accumulate all idle times (sigma_j), while t_star_i only accumulate those where x_j=1. Since x_j is either 0 or 1, t_star_i will always be less than or equal to t_i.
steps: By definition, t_i = t_1 + sum_j_from_1_to_i-1 (t_j+1 - t_j).
Also, t_j+1 - t_j >= sigma_j (the idle time in that interval).
So, t_i >= t_1 + sum_j_from_1_to_i-1 (sigma_j).
By definition, t_star_i = t_1 + sum_j_from_1_to_i-1 (x_j * sigma_j).
Since x_j is either 0 or 1, sum(x_j * sigma_j) <= sum(sigma_j).
Therefore, t_star_i <= t_i.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def check_t_star_relation(t_i, t_star_i):
    return t_star_i <= t_i
key_insights: This lemma confirms that the artificial time points provide a 'compressed' view of the timeline, which is useful for deriving upper bounds.
It ensures that shifting the time axis from t_j to t_star_j does not invalidate the workload bounds.

formal_description.statement: For all t | t_star_k <= t < f_k, C_k + sum_j_from_1_to_k_minus_1 (x_j * W_1_j(t - t_star_j) + (1 - x_j) * W_0_j(t - t_star_j)) > t - t_star_k.

variables.t_star_k: artificial time point for task k
variables.f_k: finishing time of J_k in Psi_1
variables.C_k: worst-case execution time of task k
variables.x_j: binary variable (0 or 1) for task j
variables.W_1_j_t_minus_t_star_j: workload function for task j over interval (t - t_star_j)
variables.W_0_j_t_minus_t_star_j: worst-case workload function for task j over interval (t - t_star_j)

assumptions: J_k is the job of task k under analysis
formal_description.conclusion: This inequality is a transformed version of Lemma 10's second part (Eq. 11), using the artificial time points t_star_j and removing the sigma_j terms.

informal_sketch.intuition: By shifting the time axis from t_j to t_star_j, we can 'absorb' the sigma_j terms into the interval length. Since t_star_j <= t_j, the interval (t - t_star_j) is larger than (t - t_j), which means the workload functions W_1_j and W_0_j will be greater or equal, maintaining the inequality.
steps: Start with Eq. (11) from Lemma 10.
Use Lemma 12 (t_star_j <= t_j) to show that W_1_j(t - t_j) <= W_1_j(t - t_star_j) and W_0_j(t - t_j) <= W_0_j(t - t_star_j) because workload functions are non-decreasing.
Substitute these into Eq. (11).
Rearrange terms using the definition of t_star_k (t_star_k = t_1 + sum_j_from_1_to_k-1 (x_j * sigma_j)) to eliminate sigma_j and express the right-hand side as t - t_star_k.
The strict inequality is preserved.
key_insights: This lemma is a crucial intermediate step, transforming the complex workload equation into a form that is easier to work with for deriving the final response time bound.
It effectively 'normalizes' the start time of the busy period to t_star_k.

dependencies: Definition: Task Sets T_0 and T_1

formal_description.statement: X_j is sum_l_from_j_to_k_minus_1 (x_l * sigma_l).

variables.X_j: accumulated idle time from task j to k-1, weighted by x_l
variables.x_l: binary variable (0 or 1) for task l
variables.sigma_l: amount of idle time in [t_l, t_l+1) in Psi_1
variables.k: index of the task under analysis

formal_description.conclusion: Defines a cumulative idle time term, similar to Q_x_i but using sigma_l instead of S_l.

informal_sketch.intuition: This term represents the total 'active' idle time from tasks with priority higher than or equal to tau_j (up to tau_k-1). It's used to relate the time difference (t - t_star_j) to (t - t_star_k).
steps: For a given task tau_j, iterate through all higher-priority tasks from tau_j up to tau_k-1.
If x_l for task tau_l is 1, add its idle time sigma_l to the sum.
This sum is X_j.
key_insights: X_j helps in the algebraic manipulation to derive the final response time equation.
It connects the relative time points (t - t_star_j) to a common reference (t - t_star_k).

dependencies: Definition: Task Sets T_0 and T_1

formal_description.statement: For all theta | 0 <= theta < f_k - t_star_k, C_k + sum_j_from_1_to_k_minus_1 (floor((theta + X_j + (1 - x_j)*(R_j - C_j)) / T_j) * C_j) > theta.

variables.f_k: finishing time of J_k in Psi_1
variables.t_star_k: artificial time point for task k
variables.C_k: worst-case execution time of task k
variables.X_j: accumulated idle time from task j to k-1, weighted by x_l
variables.x_j: binary variable (0 or 1) for task j
variables.R_j: worst-case response time of task j
variables.C_j: worst-case execution time of task j

assumptions: J_k is the job of task k under analysis
formal_description.conclusion: This inequality provides a lower bound on the response time of J_k, stating that if J_k has not finished by time theta, the total demand must exceed theta.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the final form of the busy-period equation for the unifying framework. It states that if task tau_k is still running at time 'theta' (relative to t_star_k), then the total demand from tau_k and all higher-priority tasks (modeled with X_j and R_j-C_j terms) must be greater than 'theta'.
steps: Start with Lemma 13: C_k + sum_j_from_1_to_k_minus_1 (x_j * W_1_j(t - t_star_j) + (1 - x_j) * W_0_j(t - t_star_j)) > t - t_star_k.
Substitute t - t_star_k with theta.
Use the relationship t - t_star_j = (t - t_star_k) + X_j = theta + X_j.
Apply the upper bounds from Lemma 11 for W_1_j and W_0_j.
Combine terms: x_j * floor((theta + X_j) / T_j) * C_j + (1 - x_j) * floor((theta + X_j + R_j - C_j) / T_j) * C_j.
Since x_j is 0 or 1, this simplifies to the given formula.
The floor function is explicitly added for consistency with job counting in RTA.
key_insights: This lemma provides the fundamental inequality that defines the response time for the new framework.
It combines elements of jitter (R_j - C_j) and carry-in (X_j) based on the x_j vector.
The smallest theta for which this inequality *does not* hold (i.e., LHS <= theta) gives the response time.

dependencies: Definition: Task Sets T_0 and T_1

formal_description.statement: Suppose that all tasks tau_i | 1 <= i <= k are schedulable (i.e., R_i <= T_i). Then, for any arbitrary vector assignment x = (x_1, x_2, ..., x_k-1), in which x_i is either 0 or 1, the worst-case response time R_k of tau_k is upper bounded by the minimum t larger than 0 such that C_k + S_k + sum_i_from_1_to_k_minus_1 (floor((t + Q_x_i + (1 - x_i)*(R_i - C_i)) / T_i) * C_i) <= t.

variables.R_k: worst-case response time of task k
variables.C_k: worst-case execution time of task k
variables.S_k: worst-case self-suspension time of task k
variables.Q_x_i: accumulated suspension term for task i based on vector x
variables.x_i: binary variable (0 or 1) for task i
variables.R_i: worst-case response time of task i
variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i
variables.k: index of the task under analysis

assumptions: R_i <= T_i for all tau_i | 1 <= i <= k (all tasks are schedulable within their periods)
formal_description.conclusion: Provides an upper bound on the WCRT of tau_k for a given x vector, by finding the smallest t that satisfies the busy-period equation.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem states that if all tasks (including tau_k) are schedulable within their periods, then the response time of tau_k can be found by solving a busy-period equation. The equation incorporates the new unified interference model using Q_x_i and (R_i - C_i) terms, which are derived from the analysis in Lemma 14.
steps: Assume a schedule where J_k misses its deadline (R_k > T_k).
Apply the schedule reduction steps (Lemmas 1-4) to get Psi_1.
Derive Lemma 14, which states that if J_k has not finished by time theta, then the demand must exceed theta.
The smallest theta for which the demand is less than or equal to theta is the response time.
Replace X_j with its upper bound Q_x_j (X_j <= Q_x_j) to get a safe upper bound for R_k.
The equation is an iterative fixed-point equation, commonly solved by starting with t = C_k + S_k and iterating until convergence or t > D_k.
key_insights: This theorem provides the core response time analysis equation for the new framework.
The x vector allows for flexible modeling of higher-priority task suspensions, combining aspects of jitter and blocking.
It's an iterative equation, typical for response time analysis.

dependencies: Definition: Task Sets T_0 and T_1
Assumption: Stronger Higher Priority Tasks Schedulability

formal_description.statement: Suppose that tau_k is not schedulable (i.e., R_k > T_k). For any arbitrary vector assignment x = (x_1, x_2, ..., x_k-1), in which x_i is either 0 or 1, we have for all t | 0 < t <= T_k, C_k + S_k + sum_i_from_1_to_k_minus_1 (floor((t + Q_x_i + (1 - x_i)*(R_i - C_i)) / T_i) * C_i) > t.

variables.R_k: worst-case response time of task k
variables.C_k: worst-case execution time of task k
variables.S_k: worst-case self-suspension time of task k
variables.Q_x_i: accumulated suspension term for task i based on vector x
variables.x_i: binary variable (0 or 1) for task i
variables.R_i: worst-case response time of task i
variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i
variables.k: index of the task under analysis

assumptions: R_i <= T_i for all tau_i | 1 <= i < k (higher priority tasks are schedulable within their periods)
formal_description.conclusion: If tau_k is unschedulable (R_k > T_k), then the busy-period equation (from Theorem 1) will not find a solution t <= T_k.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem is the contrapositive of Theorem 1, or rather, it states that if a task misses its deadline (specifically, its response time exceeds its period), then the busy-period equation will not converge to a value within its period. This is important for proving the correctness of the schedulability test.
steps: Assume J_k is the first job of tau_k that misses its deadline, meaning R_k > T_k.
Apply the schedule reduction steps (Lemmas 1-4) to this scenario.
The derivation of Lemma 14 still holds, showing that for any theta < f_k - t_star_k, the demand exceeds theta.
Since f_k - t_star_k > T_k (because R_k > T_k and t_star_k <= r_k), this means the demand will exceed theta for all theta up to T_k.
Therefore, the equation will not find a solution t <= T_k.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def check_unschedulable_condition(task_k, hp_tasks, x_vector, hp_R_values):
    # If calculate_R_k_upper_bound returns float('inf') or a value > task_k.T
    # then this condition holds.
    R_k_bound = calculate_R_k_upper_bound(task_k, hp_tasks, x_vector, hp_R_values)
    return R_k_bound > task_k.T
key_insights: This theorem provides the 'completeness' aspect of the schedulability test: if a task is truly unschedulable, the test will reflect it.
It ensures that the response time analysis is not overly optimistic.

Assumption: Stronger Higher Priority Tasks Schedulability

formal_description.statement: If for all tau_i | 1 <= i < k, R_i <= T_i, and if there is a vector x = (x_1, x_2, ..., x_k-1) with x_i in {0, 1}, such that there exists a time t | 0 < t <= D_k, and C_k + S_k + sum_i_from_1_to_k_minus_1 (floor((t + Q_x_i + (1 - x_i)*(R_i - C_i)) / T_i) * C_i) <= t, then the constrained-deadline task tau_k is schedulable under fixed-priority.

variables.R_i: worst-case response time of task i
variables.C_k: worst-case execution time of task k
variables.S_k: worst-case self-suspension time of task k
variables.Q_x_i: accumulated suspension term for task i based on vector x
variables.x_i: binary variable (0 or 1) for task i

assumptions: R_i <= T_i for all tau_i | 1 <= i < k (higher priority tasks are schedulable within their periods)
formal_description.conclusion: A task tau_k is schedulable if there exists at least one binary vector x for which its response time (calculated by the unifying framework) is less than or equal to its deadline D_k.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the practical schedulability test derived from Theorems 1 and 2. It says that if you can find *any* way to model the higher-priority suspensions (by choosing an x vector) such that tau_k finishes by its deadline, then tau_k is schedulable.
steps: For each higher-priority task tau_i, calculate its R_i (using any valid method, potentially recursively applying this corollary).
Iterate through all possible 2^(k-1) binary vectors 'x'.
For each 'x' vector, calculate the response time R_k_x for task tau_k using the iterative equation from Theorem 1.
If for any 'x', R_k_x is found to be less than or equal to D_k, then tau_k is schedulable.
If after checking all 'x' vectors, no such R_k_x is found, then tau_k is not schedulable.
key_insights: This corollary is the main contribution of the paper, providing a unifying and dominating schedulability test.
The search over 'x' vectors allows the analysis to adapt to the specific interference pattern that maximizes tau_k's response time.
It analytically dominates previous methods because it can choose the 'best' x vector that yields the tightest bound.

results.identifier: Lemma 15: Dominance of Eq (3) over Eq (1)

formal_description.statement: The schedulability test of task tau_k provided by Eq. (3) dominates that of Eq. (1).
formal_description.conclusion: If a task set is deemed schedulable by the Suspension-Oblivious test (Eq. 1), it will also be deemed schedulable by the Blocking Time test (Eq. 3).

informal_sketch.intuition: The blocking time model (Eq. 3) is generally more accurate than the suspension-oblivious model (Eq. 1) because it accounts for the fact that a higher-priority task's suspension doesn't always cause as much interference as its full computation time.
steps: Compare the interference terms in Eq. (1) and Eq. (3).
Eq. (1) uses (C_i + S_i) for higher-priority tasks.
Eq. (3) uses C_i for higher-priority tasks, and moves S_i (and min(C_i, S_i) from hp tasks) into B_k.
The proof shows that sum_i_from_1_to_k_minus_1 (floor(t / T_i) * C_i) + B_k <= sum_i_from_1_to_k_minus_1 (floor(t / T_i) * (C_i + S_i)) + S_k.
Specifically, min(C_i, S_i) <= S_i, so the blocking term B_k is generally smaller than the sum of all S_i terms if they were added to C_i.

This means the left-hand side of Eq. (3) is less than or equal to the left-hand side of Eq. (1) for any given t, implying Eq. (3) will find a solution (if one exists) that is smaller or equal, thus dominating.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def check_dominance_eq3_over_eq1(task_k, hp_tasks):
    # This is a theoretical proof, not a direct code check.
    # It implies that if check_suspension_oblivious_schedulability(task_k, hp_tasks) is True,
    # then check_blocking_schedulability(task_k, hp_tasks, calculate_blocking_time(task_k, hp_tasks)) must also be True.
    pass
key_insights: This lemma confirms that the blocking time approach is a refinement over the simpler suspension-oblivious approach.
It's part of the paper's broader argument that the new unifying framework dominates all existing correct analyses.
